definition: The environmental impact of the design, training, deployment and use of artificial intelligence includes the greenhouse gas emissions from generating electricity for data centres and computing hardware, operational and upstream water use, and material impacts from hardware manufacturing, mining and electronic waste.
details: Estimating AI's environmental effects can be difficult because results depend on how impacts are measured, including whether accounting includes only model computation or also data-centre overhead, idle capacity, hardware manufacture, and local electricity supply. As these issues have received greater attention, governments and regulators have increasingly considered data-centre reporting requirements, energy-efficiency standards, and broader transparency measures for AI-related resource use.

explainer.lead: AI affects the environment not only while a model is running, but also through the electricity, water and physical hardware needed to build and operate it. Looking across this whole chain helps governments, operators and users compare impacts and decide where reporting or efficiency measures are needed.

tiers.eli5: Using AI is a bit like running a busy kitchen: the cooking uses power and water, but making the equipment and throwing old equipment away also have effects. To understand AI's footprint, we have to count the computers, the buildings around them and where their electricity comes from—not just the moment an answer appears.
tiers.practitioner: In practice, assessments define a system boundary before estimating electricity emissions, operational and upstream water use, and hardware-related impacts. A compute-only measurement can differ substantially from one that includes data-centre overhead, idle capacity, manufacturing and the local electricity supply, so comparisons need matching scopes and transparent assumptions.
tiers.paperLevel: An operational estimate can be written as electricity-related impact = f(electricity consumption, local electricity supply), with consumption potentially covering model computation, data-centre overhead and idle capacity. A broader assessment additionally accounts for operational and upstream water use plus material impacts from manufacturing, mining and electronic waste. Estimates are sensitive to these accounting boundaries and are not directly comparable when their scopes differ.

explainer.example: Two assessments examine the same AI training run. The first counts only model computation, while the second also includes data-centre overhead, idle capacity, hardware manufacture and the local electricity supply; their results can differ because their boundaries differ, even though the training run is identical.

usedIn.name: Data-centre reporting
usedIn.detail: Structures disclosure of resource use associated with AI computing.

usedIn.name: Energy-efficiency standards
usedIn.detail: Provides a basis for considering how efficiently AI infrastructure uses electricity.

usedIn.name: AI transparency measures
usedIn.detail: Supports broader reporting of AI-related resource consumption and environmental effects.

usedIn.name: Hardware lifecycle assessment
usedIn.detail: Extends analysis beyond operation to manufacturing, mining and electronic waste.

explainer.intuition: An AI answer has a physical footprint behind it: machines must be manufactured, supplied with electricity and sometimes water, and eventually disposed of. The measured footprint depends on how much of that chain is included.
howItWorks: Identify the AI activity being assessed, such as design, training, deployment or use.
Measure electricity demand, deciding whether to include data-centre overhead and idle capacity as well as computation.
Account for the local electricity supply and for operational and upstream water use.
Include hardware manufacturing, mining and electronic waste when using a broader lifecycle boundary.
Report the accounting choices so that estimates with different scopes are not treated as equivalent.
explainer.whyItMatters: Clear accounting makes the trade-offs behind AI infrastructure visible and supports decisions about reporting requirements, energy-efficiency standards and transparency. It also prevents narrow measurements from being mistaken for a complete environmental assessment.
misconceptions: The environmental impact is not limited to electricity used by model computation.
Water use and hardware impacts can extend beyond day-to-day operation.
Two footprint estimates are not necessarily comparable if their accounting boundaries differ.

diagram.caption: AI's environmental footprint spans infrastructure operation, electricity and water use, and the hardware lifecycle.
